short.label: About 50 words
short.text: Margaya is an open-source project management platform for teams that want clear ownership without heavy process. Plan work on boards, lists, spreadsheets, calendars and Gantt charts, write docs beside the tasks, and connect your tools through a REST API and MCP. Run it on your own server, free and open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0.

long.label: About 150 words
long.text: Margaya is an open-source project management platform built for teams that want to plan and ship work without the tool becoming a job of its own. Tasks move through board, list, spreadsheet, calendar and Gantt views of the same data. Cycles, modules, estimates and an intake inbox are there when a team needs planning, and stay out of the way when it doesn't. Teams write docs together next to their tasks, collect requests on public boards, and follow progress with analytics and an audit log. A REST API with an OpenAPI description, webhooks, an MCP server and integrations with GitHub, Gitea, Slack, Discord and others connect Margaya to the rest of a team's tools. The interface is available in 20 languages. Margaya is released under the GNU AGPL-3.0, with a commercial licence for use without its conditions, and runs on a single server with Docker, or on Kubernetes with Helm.

hero.caption: Type a task with @person, !priority and #label, and Margaya turns them into properties.
hero.description: Demo: a cursor types “Fix login redirect @adam !high #bug” into the To do capture bar. Chips for Adam Reyes, High priority and the bug label appear. Enter adds the task to To do. The task is dragged to In progress, and a click opens the task sheet with its status, priority, assignee and label.

viewBoard.caption: Drag a card to another column, and its status follows.
viewBoard.description: Demo: on the Website board, the card “Rotate API tokens” is dragged from In progress to In review.

viewList.caption: Group by status, fold away what is done, and select tasks to change them together.
viewList.description: Demo: in the list layout, grouped by status, the Done group is collapsed. Two tasks in progress are selected with their checkboxes, and a toolbar offers actions for both at once. The Done group then opens again.

viewSpreadsheet.caption: Every property is a cell you can edit in place.
viewSpreadsheet.description: Demo: in the spreadsheet layout, a click on the Priority cell of “Cut dashboard load time” opens the priority picker, and Urgent replaces Medium.

viewCalendar.caption: Drag a task to another day to reschedule it, then zoom in on the week.
viewCalendar.description: Demo: on the October calendar, “Fix focus order in dialogs” is dragged from October 14 to October 16. The calendar then switches from Month to Week and shows the week of October 12 with each task's assignees.

viewGantt.caption: Zoom out, follow the dependencies, and stretch a bar to change its dates.
viewGantt.description: Demo: the Gantt chart zooms from Week to Month. A line appears from “Rotate API tokens” to “Write the 2.4 release notes”, the task it blocks. The end of the first bar is dragged two days later, so it now ends after the blocked task starts: the line turns red and the task list flags the conflict.

palette.caption: Ctrl K runs any command. Here it changes the open task's status without the mouse.
palette.description: Demo: with a task open in the side sheet, Ctrl K opens the command bar. Typing “> status” narrows it to actions and shows “Change status…” for this task. Enter opens the status picker, the down arrow moves to In progress, and Enter applies it. A toast confirms “Status changed”.

cycles.caption: Cycles show progress as it happens: finish a task and the burn-down moves.
cycles.description: Demo: the Cycle 12 page of the Website project. Its tasks are listed by status beside the cycle sidebar, which shows 55% progress, 16 of 30 points and a burn-down chart that draws itself against the ideal line. The cursor opens the status of “Cache avatar images” and picks Done. The task joins the Done group, progress rises to 64% and the chart drops to 4 tasks left.

modules.caption: Modules group the bigger pieces of work, each with a lead, dates and progress.
modules.description: Demo: the Modules page lists six modules with progress rings, status chips and lead avatars. The cursor switches to the gallery layout, where each module shows a progress bar, then changes Mobile onboarding from Planned to In progress.

estimates.caption: Estimates appear as chips on tasks and add up in cycles and modules.
estimates.description: A points estimate system with the values 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13, and four tasks with point chips. A summary shows 13 of 26 points done.

intake.caption: Triage requests from the keyboard: J and K move, A accepts, D declines.
intake.description: Demo: the Intake queue of the Website project with four requests. J and K move the selection. A opens the accept dialog and “Export invoices as PDF” is accepted into To do. J moves on, D opens the decline dialog, a reason is typed, and “Play confetti when a task is done” is declined with that reason.

inbox.caption: The inbox keeps notifications in one place: snooze what can wait, mark the rest read.
inbox.description: Demo: the inbox with five notifications, three of them unread. The cursor snoozes Jonas Berg’s assignment until tomorrow, and it leaves the list. Then it marks Mira Okafor’s mention as read, and the unread count drops.

home.caption: Home starts your day with quick links, recent visits and private stickies.
home.description: Demo: the Home page greets Adam Reyes and shows shortcuts to the inbox, Your work and stickies, then quick links and recent visits. The cursor scrolls to Stickies, adds a sticky and types a note into it.

yourWork.caption: Your work collects what is assigned to you, what you created and what you follow.
yourWork.description: Demo: the Your work page. The cursor moves through the Assigned, Created and Subscribed tabs, and each lists its own tasks across projects with status, priority and due dates.

digest.caption: The daily digest, by email.
digest.description: An email preview titled “Your daily digest”: for the Northwind workspace, two tasks due soon and one overdue, two new mentions and four unread notifications, with an Open inbox button.

docs.caption: Write together, insert a callout with a slash, and paste a task link to get a live chip.
docs.description: Demo: the page Launch plan is open, with the project's page tree on the left and a Live stack showing Mira Okafor. Adam types in one paragraph while Mira's cursor, with her name tag, types in another. Adam types a slash, narrows the menu to Callout and inserts an info callout. Then he pastes a task link, which becomes a chip with the task key and title.

docsTogether.caption: Two people, one page, no conflicts: every edit shows up as it is typed.
docsTogether.description: Demo: on the page Launch plan, Adam types in one paragraph while Mira Okafor's cursor, with her name tag, types in another at the same time. The Live stack in the top bar shows who is on the page.

docsSlash.caption: Type a slash to insert headings, lists, tables, code or a callout.
docsSlash.description: Demo: Adam types a slash on an empty line. The block menu opens with Text, Lists and Insert groups. He narrows it to Callout and presses Enter, and an info callout appears for him to type into.

docsTasks.caption: Paste a task link and it becomes a chip with the task's key, title and status.
docsTasks.description: Demo: Adam pastes a task link at the end of a sentence. It turns into a chip showing WEB-31 and its title. Pointing at the chip shows a preview with the assignee, status and priority.

analytics.caption: Group tasks by status, priority, assignee or label, and the chart rebuilds.
analytics.description: Demo: in Analytics, a custom chart shows tasks by priority. The cursor opens the X-axis menu and picks Status. The bars regrow to show Backlog, To do, In progress, In review and Done counts.

auditLog.caption: Every change to members, roles, keys, webhooks and integrations is on record.
auditLog.description: Demo: the workspace audit log lists time, actor, action and target. New entries arrive at the top: an API key created, Slack connected, a webhook changed by an API key.

trash.caption: Deleted by mistake? Restore the task, with its sub-tasks, in one click.

integrations.caption: Git hosting, chat, push notifications, webhooks, a REST API and MCP.

api.caption: Every action in the app is a documented REST call, described with OpenAPI.
api.description: A curl command that creates a task: POST to /api/task/ followed by the project id, with an API key as a Bearer token and a JSON body with the title, description, priority and status. The response returns the created task.

mcp.caption: Connect an AI agent over MCP and it works with the same tasks you do.

jira.caption: Moving from Jira? Upload its CSV export, map the statuses, and import.

ask.caption: Ask about the work, then let Build make the change. You confirm it.

The assistant lists what it read, thinks for two seconds and answers: WEB-5 and WEB-6 are blocked, and WEB-5 has no assignee. Switched to Build, they ask it to assign WEB-5 to Mira. selfHost.question: Can I host Margaya myself?
selfHost.answer: Yes. Run it with Docker Compose on a single server, or on Kubernetes with the official Helm chart. You need one app container and a PostgreSQL database. The install guide covers environment variables, storage and reverse proxies.

redis.question: Do I need Redis or other extra services?
redis.answer: No. A single server works without Redis. Redis is optional and only needed when you run several API instances and want realtime updates to reach every one of them.

data.question: Who owns my data?
data.answer: You do. Margaya runs only on your own server, so nothing leaves your infrastructure and we receive no data from it. You can export tasks to CSV, Excel or JSON at any time.

license.question: What licence is Margaya under?
license.answer: The GNU AGPL-3.0. You can use, change and host Margaya for free. If you modify it and let people use it over a network, you publish your changes under the same licence. To use Margaya without those conditions, for example to keep your changes private or build it into a closed product, you can get a commercial licence. Single sign-on, the audit log, the API and MCP are all in the open-source build.

cost.question: What does it cost?
cost.answer: Self-hosting Margaya under the AGPL-3.0 is free, with every feature included. Businesses that need to use it without the AGPL's conditions, such as keeping their changes private, can buy a commercial licence.

languages.question: Which languages does the app support?
languages.answer: The interface is available in 20 languages, and each person can choose their own.

jira.question: Can I move my work over from Jira?
jira.answer: Yes. Import the CSV file Jira exports, then map its statuses, priorities and people to your project. Margaya never connects to your Jira site, so no Jira token is needed. A generic CSV import covers other tools.

api.question: Is there an API, and does it work with AI agents?
api.answer: Every instance has a REST API described with OpenAPI, plus API keys and outgoing webhooks. A built-in MCP endpoint lets AI agents read and update tasks as the person who approved them.

ai.question: Does Margaya have AI, and is it on by default?
ai.answer: Yes, and no. Ask AI, Build mode, writing help, triage suggestions and AI agents are built in, but they stay off until an instance admin connects a model and a workspace turns AI on. Every change the AI proposes is shown to you first and can be undone.

aiData.question: Which AI models can I use, and where does my data go?
aiData.answer: Use Claude, or any OpenAI-compatible model you run yourself, such as Ollama or vLLM. With local-only routing nothing leaves your network. Margaya only sends what the person asking can already see, keeps no prompts or answers unless you turn on server history, and records usage counts for budgets.

history.title: History, locks and private drafts
history.body: Restore earlier versions, lock finished pages and keep private pages that only you can see.

cta.title: Keep the why next to the what.
cta.description: Pages are on by default in every project.

automate.metaTitle: Integrations, REST API, MCP and Jira import
automate.metaDescription: Connect Margaya to GitHub, Gitea, Slack, Discord, Telegram, Mattermost and webhooks, script it with a documented REST API, let AI agents work through MCP, and import from Jira.
automate.title: Connect the tools you already use.
automate.description: Integrations, a documented API and a built-in MCP endpoint, all included in the open-source build.

integrations.title: Integrations and webhooks
integrations.body: Link pull requests from GitHub or Gitea, send updates to Slack, Discord, Telegram or Mattermost, and post events to any URL with outgoing webhooks.

api.title: A REST API with OpenAPI
api.body: Everything the app does goes through the same documented API. Create API keys and script it from any language.

mcp.title: MCP for AI agents
mcp.body: Every instance serves an MCP endpoint. Agents ask for your approval first, then create and update tasks as you.

jira.title: Import from Jira
jira.body: Upload Jira's CSV export, map statuses, priorities and people, and bring over sub-tasks, links and comments.

cleanup.title: Automation rules
cleanup.body: Set up When, If, Then rules for routine work, such as assigning or labelling new tasks, and archive or close stale tasks on a schedule, with a preview of what each rule will touch.

cta.title: Make Margaya part of your stack.
cta.description: Read the API reference, or connect your first integration in minutes.

ai.metaTitle: AI assistant, Build mode and agents
ai.metaDescription: Ask questions about your work and get answers from live data, let Build mode propose changes you confirm, write with AI help and assign tasks to AI agents, with your own model and AI off by default.
ai.title: An assistant that knows the work.
ai.description: Ask AI, Build mode, writing help and agents, all in the open-source build, running on the model you choose.

ask.title: Ask AI
ask.body: Ask in plain words and get answers from live tasks, with counts, charts and links to the tasks and pages it used. Mention a task, page or person with @, attach a file, or speak instead of typing.

build.title: Build mode
build.body: Describe a change, such as a project with three tasks or a task for Mia. You see what it read and how it reasoned, edit the proposed changes, confirm them, and undo any of them for an hour.

writing.title: Writing help
writing.body: Improve, shorten, translate or change the tone of a description or comment, get a title suggestion, summarise a task, or add an AI block to a page.

triage.title: Triage and briefs
triage.body: Get label and priority suggestions for new work, spot duplicates, filter a board by describing what you want, and get a summary of your unread inbox or a brief for a cycle.

agents.title: AI agents
agents.body: Agents are members you can assign tasks to. They ask a person when stuck, wait for approval before writing, run on a schedule, and can use tools from other MCP servers you connect.

privacy.title: Your model, your rules
privacy.body: AI is off until an admin turns it on. Use Claude or a local model, keep data on your network, set budgets, and keep no prompts or answers unless you choose to.

cta.title: Turn on AI when you are ready.
cta.description: Read the AI setup guide, or try Ask AI in a workspace of your own.

selfHost.metaTitle: Self-host Margaya with Docker or Helm
selfHost.metaDescription: Run Margaya on your own server with Docker Compose or Kubernetes with Helm. PostgreSQL only, Redis optional, AGPL-3.0 licensed, with trash, audit log and full exports.
selfHost.title: Run it yourself, keep everything.
selfHost.description: One app container and PostgreSQL. Every feature included, no feature gates, and nothing sent back to us.

deploy.title: Docker Compose or Helm
deploy.body: Start with Docker Compose on a single server, or deploy the official Helm chart to Kubernetes.

scale.title: Single server first, Redis when you scale
scale.body: One instance needs nothing but PostgreSQL. Add Redis only when several API instances must share realtime updates.

safety.title: Trash and audit log
safety.body: Deleted work waits in the trash for 30 days, and the audit log records who changed members, roles, keys and settings.

ownership.title: Your data, in open formats
ownership.body: Export tasks to CSV, Excel or JSON, sign in with your own OIDC provider, and keep backups wherever you like.

cta.title: Have it running in minutes.
cta.description: Follow the install guide and run Margaya on your own server.

campaign-management.name: Campaign management
campaign-management.pitch: Plan each campaign, see what is live, and keep budget and results next to the work.
campaign-management.description: A board for marketing teams running several campaigns at once. Each campaign is a module, each channel piece a task, and a separate Live status shows what is running right now. Every piece carries its budget, a target written before launch and the result recorded after.

community-management.name: Community management
community-management.pitch: Welcome members, handle problems fast, and turn their ideas into action.
community-management.description: One place to look after a community of members, customers or volunteers. Members share feedback, event ideas and problems through a simple form, moderation cases jump to the top, and a monthly health check shows how the community is doing.

content-calendar.name: Content calendar
content-calendar.pitch: See what goes out when, and where every piece stands on its way there.
content-calendar.description: Plan articles, social posts, videos and newsletters on one calendar. Ideas wait in their own bank until they get a writer and a publish date, the statuses show how far along each piece is, and the live link on every published card turns the calendar into an archive.

cross-team-planning.name: Shared team plan
cross-team-planning.pitch: Common goals, clear owners, visible dependencies.
cross-team-planning.description: Plan a quarter or half-year across several teams. Each team adds what it will deliver toward a few shared goals, marks it committed or stretch with an honest confidence level, and links the work it depends on. A timeline, a dependencies view and a weekly update keep everyone aligned without extra meetings.

customer-support.name: Customer support
customer-support.pitch: Questions, bugs and ideas from customers, sorted and answered.
customer-support.description: A support desk that sorts every message at the door: questions get answered, real bugs go to engineering and ideas are collected for later. Tier labels send hard cases to specialists, a count of customers asking turns duplicates into a signal, and a known issues page keeps answers consistent.

design-request-desk.name: Design request desk
design-request-desk.pitch: Clear asks, focused reviews, clean hand-offs.
design-request-desk.description: Collect design asks with a goal, a format and a date through one request form. The team sizes and assigns each request, shares concepts in a review step and hands off the final files without an endless thread.

development-requests.name: Requests for engineering
development-requests.pitch: One front door for every ask.
development-requests.description: Give other teams one form for everything they need from engineering. Requests are reviewed on a fixed rhythm, accepted work is scheduled when there is room, and requesters hear back automatically when it is delivered.

document-review.name: Document review
document-review.pitch: Get documents reviewed, revised and signed off, always on the right version.
document-review.description: Take contracts, procedures and reports through review rounds to a final sign-off. Each document keeps its file, version and round on one task, so nobody comments on an old copy. High-risk documents get their own view, and signed-off versions stay frozen.

email-campaign.name: Email campaigns
email-campaign.pitch: Every email from brief to send, with a real QA step and the results kept on the card.
email-campaign.description: Each newsletter, promotion or announcement is one card, from a short brief through copy, design and a QA check before it is scheduled. After sending, the card waits in Sent until its open and click rates are written on it, so you build a history of what works.

employee-reviews.name: Employee reviews
employee-reviews.pitch: Run a review cycle on time, from self-review to conversation, without putting anyone's rating on the board.
employee-reviews.description: One card per employee, named by an employee code, moves from self-review through manager review, calibration and the review conversation. The project is private by default: ratings, pay and written feedback stay in the HR system, so the board shows progress and nothing more.

event-planning.name: Event planning
event-planning.pitch: From venue search to thank-you notes, every booking, deadline and cost for one event.
event-planning.description: Plan a conference, meetup or workshop backwards from the date. Vendor bookings carry their cost and contract status, so the budget sheet stays current, and anything waiting on a reply gets a follow-up date by itself. A countdown shows what is left, and the run of show page carries the day itself.

facilities-service-desk.name: Facilities service desk
facilities-service-desk.pitch: Repairs, moves, cleaning and event setups for your buildings, scheduled and tracked from report to done.
facilities-service-desk.description: Take building issues and booking requests from anyone through a simple form, sort them by urgency and track each one from report to done. Planned work such as desk moves and event setups has its own Scheduled column and calendar, and safety hazards jump the queue.

finance-service-desk.name: Finance service desk
finance-service-desk.pitch: Purchases, claims and invoices, approved and paid on time.
finance-service-desk.description: One queue for purchase requests, expense claims, supplier invoices and budget questions. Every request arrives with its type, amount and cost center, approval has its own status, and a view sorted by amount shows what still needs a yes before the books close.

financial-close.name: Financial close
financial-close.pitch: A month-end checklist that rebuilds itself every month, with a reviewer on every step.
financial-close.description: A month-end close board for accounting teams of any size. Every close step repeats on its own day of the month, is grouped by close day and waits in a review queue until someone other than the preparer checks it. A sign-off page records who locked the period and when.

general-service-desk.name: General service desk
general-service-desk.pitch: One front door for every kind of request, sorted and answered from a single queue.
general-service-desk.description: Collect questions and asks for IT, people, money and buildings in one place. Each request is reviewed in triage, gets a team and a priority from its impact and urgency, and a due date follows on its own. A short knowledge base keeps the same questions from coming back.

go-to-market.name: Go-to-market launch
go-to-market.pitch: One board for everything that has to be true before, on and after launch day.
go-to-market.description: A launch board for product marketers and launch leads, from about eight weeks out to a month after. Work is split by phase, go/no-go items are flagged so the readiness view becomes the meeting agenda, and a weekly project update keeps stakeholders informed.

grant-tracker.name: Grant tracker
grant-tracker.pitch: Every funding opportunity from first look to final report, with no deadline missed.
grant-tracker.description: Track each grant as a card with its funder, amount and deadline, from the first look through the letter of inquiry, the application and the decision. Awarded grants stay open until the final report is accepted, and declined ones keep their feedback for the next round.

hr-service-desk.name: HR service desk
hr-service-desk.pitch: A private queue for people requests, starters and leavers.
hr-service-desk.description: Questions about pay, leave and policies, plus new starters and leavers, in one restricted queue that only the HR team sees. The request form asks only what's needed, onboarding and offboarding steps become sub-tasks with an owner each, and sensitive cases go straight to the lead.

ip-infringement.name: IP infringement
ip-infringement.pitch: Log suspected misuse of your brand, content or inventions, decide what to do, and follow each case through to the end.
ip-infringement.description: A private case tracker for copied content, lookalike logos, counterfeit goods and claims made against you. Reports come in through a form, evidence is captured first, and each case climbs the response ladder, from a platform report to formal action, only as far as it needs to. This template organises the work; it is not legal advice.

it-asset-management.name: IT assets
it-asset-management.pitch: Every device and licence, from request to retirement.
it-asset-management.description: Track laptops, screens, phones and software subscriptions from the request that starts them to the day they're retired. A few fields keep the register easy to maintain, the due date warns you before a renewal or warranty ends, and retiring a device follows a checklist that records the data wipe and disposal.

it-operations.name: IT operations
it-operations.pitch: Alerts, incidents and changes, handled the same way every time.
it-operations.description: One board for monitoring alerts, incidents and planned changes to live systems. Severity sets the pace, every incident starts with a first-response checklist, and serious outages end in a blameless review. Changes carry a rollback plan and show on a calendar by their window.

it-service-desk.name: IT service desk
it-service-desk.pitch: Everyday IT help in one queue: fix what's broken, hand out access and equipment, and make small changes safely.
it-service-desk.description: One queue for the IT help colleagues ask for: things that are broken, access, devices, software and small changes. Requesters choose the impact and urgency on the form, you set the priority, and each priority gets its own due date. Starter pages explain how to get help and include a knowledge base and a checklist for small changes.

it-service-management.name: IT service management
it-service-management.pitch: Incidents, service requests, problems and changes in one project, each with its own label, checklist and target.
it-service-management.description: One project for the whole IT service: restore service fast after incidents, fulfil routine requests, remove the causes of repeat faults and change systems with care. Priority comes from impact and urgency, targets are set automatically, and every change carries a way to undo it.

kanban.name: Kanban flow
kanban.pitch: Keep work moving. Finish before you start.
kanban.description: A continuous-flow board for teams with a steady stream of work and no fixed sprints. Policies are written down, urgent work has its own lane, and views show what is ageing or stuck before it becomes a problem.

lead-tracking.name: Lead tracking
lead-tracking.pitch: Catch every new lead, follow up on time, and decide quickly: qualified, nurture or not a fit.
lead-tracking.description: A light board for leads from your website form, referrals and events. Form leads get a reply date the moment you accept them, each attempt sets the next follow-up, and every lead ends qualified, set aside to nurture, or closed with a reason.

legal-request-desk.name: Legal request desk
legal-request-desk.pitch: Contracts and legal questions, complete on arrival.
legal-request-desk.description: Take in contract reviews, confidentiality agreements and legal questions through one form that asks for the counterparty, value and real deadline. Standard agreements take a fast path, unusual terms get a senior look, and a With counterparty status shows when the wait is on the other side. A playbook, signing rules and a short FAQ answer simple questions before they become requests.

marketing-assets.name: Marketing asset requests
marketing-assets.pitch: One form for every graphic, banner and slide request, and one queue the design team can actually plan.
marketing-assets.description: A request desk for in-house design teams. Requesters fill in one form with the asset type, sizes, copy and date, the design lead accepts each brief from triage, and separate review and change steps show whose turn it is.

marketing-request-desk.name: Marketing request desk
marketing-request-desk.pitch: Briefs in, deliverables out, on time.
marketing-request-desk.description: Take in asks for posts, emails, pages and event support through a short brief, then plan and deliver them on time. Every request arrives with a goal, an audience, a reach and a date, so priorities between teams stay fair. A review step and a publishing calendar keep feedback clear and stop launches from colliding.

nonprofit-programs.name: Nonprofit programs
nonprofit-programs.pitch: Run your programs week to week and show what they achieved, from the same board.
nonprofit-programs.description: Plan the sessions, outreach and volunteer work of each program, and record how many people took part and how many volunteer hours it took right after each session. When the quarter ends, the outputs sheet already holds the numbers and a project update tells your board what changed.

outcome-tree.name: Outcome tree
outcome-tree.pitch: From the result you want to the tests that prove the way.
outcome-tree.description: Map a measurable outcome down to the customer needs behind it, the ideas that could meet them and the small tests that show which ideas hold up. Each level sits as a sub-task under the one above, every new solution gets a test automatically, and discarded branches stay on the tree as learning.

personal-planner.name: Personal planner
personal-planner.pitch: Today, this week, someday: a small list that gets things out of your head.
personal-planner.description: A light planner for one person. Everything lands in the Inbox first, each morning you pull a few cards into Today, and a short weekly review sorts the rest into This week or Someday. No fields, no extra features, nothing to maintain.

policy-management.name: Policy management
policy-management.pitch: Write, approve and publish policies, and never miss a yearly review.
policy-management.description: Take each company policy from request to draft, review, approval and publication, with a clear record of who approved what and when. Every policy carries an owner, a version and a review date, and repeats each year so the next review appears on its own.

portfolio-roadmap.name: Portfolio roadmap
portfolio-roadmap.pitch: Every initiative, one timeline, a balanced mix.
portfolio-roadmap.description: See every major initiative across the organisation on one timeline, grouped under the strategic goals they serve. Tag each one with an investment area to keep the mix balanced, decide on new proposals together, and bring at-risk work to the review before it slips.

prioritization.name: Priority scoring
prioritization.pitch: Compare ideas on reach, impact, confidence and effort.
prioritization.description: A shared, repeatable way to compare more good ideas than you have capacity for. Each candidate gets a reach, an impact, a confidence and an effort, and the Ranking view sorts them by score. The scoring guide keeps the scales the same from round to round.

process-control.name: Process control
process-control.pitch: Improve a process in small tested steps, then keep the gains with regular checks.
process-control.description: Run each improvement through plan, do, check and act, with the baseline and target written down before the test starts. Results sit next to their targets, adopted changes go into standard work, and recurring control checks make sure the gains hold.

procurement.name: Procurement
procurement.pitch: From "we need this" to paid in full, with every purchase approved, ordered, received and matched.
procurement.description: Collect purchase requests through one form and get each one approved before anything is ordered. Track orders until they arrive, then match the order, the delivery and the invoice before payment, so mistakes surface straight away.

product-discovery.name: Product discovery
product-discovery.pitch: Learn first, then build what's proven.
product-discovery.description: Collect ideas from customers, support, sales and your own team, then test the riskiest ones with interviews and small experiments before anyone builds them. An Evidence field shows how much you really know, and proven ideas move to delivery with their brief attached.

product-roadmap.name: Product roadmap
product-roadmap.description: A roadmap in three horizons, Now, Next and Later, with every item under a theme that says what success looks like. A confidence field shows how sure each item is, and a timeline appears only where dates are real.

project-management.name: Project management
project-management.pitch: Take a project from idea to wrap-up with clear phases, owners and milestones.
project-management.description: For a project with a start, an end and a few people who need to sign off. Work moves through four phases, milestones and risks stand out on the timeline, and a weekly update keeps everyone else informed. A short brief sets the scope up front, and closeout notes capture what the team learned.

recruitment.name: Recruitment
recruitment.pitch: Move candidates from application to hire with a fair, structured process and as little personal data as possible.
recruitment.description: A hiring pipeline for small teams filling a few roles at a time. Each candidate is one card with a reference code instead of a name, every interviewer scores on their own before the debrief, and turned-down candidates hear back within two days. The project starts restricted, so only the hiring team sees it.

rfp-process.name: RFP process
rfp-process.pitch: Run a fair request for proposals, from first draft to signed award, with every question answered for every bidder.
rfp-process.description: A competitive purchase from brief to award. Criteria and weights are fixed before any proposal is opened, every supplier question is answered for all bidders at once, and each evaluator scores alone before the panel meets.

sales-pipeline.name: Sales pipeline
sales-pipeline.pitch: Every deal as a card, every stage as a column: drag it forward when it really moves.
sales-pipeline.description: Track deals from first conversation to signed contract on a board where each column is a stage. Every deal carries its value, company and expected close date, so you can see where the money sits and what should close this month. Slipped close dates get a nudge, and every lost deal records why.

sales-support-desk.name: Sales support desk
sales-support-desk.pitch: Quotes, approvals and paperwork that help deals close.
sales-support-desk.description: A request desk for the team behind the sellers: quotes, discount approvals, contract reviews and security questionnaires. Every request carries its deal value, account and close date, so the desk helps the biggest and soonest deals first. Pricing exceptions get their own status and label, and a shared answer library speeds up questionnaires.

sample-playground.name: Guided tour
sample-playground.pitch: Learn Margaya by doing, in eight short stops.
sample-playground.description: A practice project where every task is a short lesson. Eight numbered stops walk you through moving a task, making a view, planning a cycle, grouping work into a module, writing on a page and sketching on a whiteboard. Nothing here is real work, so keep it as a sandbox or delete it when you are done.

scrum.name: Scrum sprints
scrum.pitch: One goal per sprint. Plan, build, review, improve.
scrum.description: Work in short, fixed sprints built around one goal. Size stories in points, commit to what fits, and let unfinished work roll into the next sprint on its own. A shared Definition of Done and a team working agreement keep everyone on the same page.

task-tracking.name: Task tracking
task-tracking.pitch: A simple shared list of who is doing what, and by when.
task-tracking.description: A light board for everyday work: every task has an owner, a due date and a priority, and nothing more to fill in. A Waiting column keeps stalled work apart from work not yet started, and overdue tasks flag themselves.

top-level-planning.name: Program plan
top-level-planning.pitch: Initiatives, milestones and risks on one timeline.
top-level-planning.description: A multi-month program split into a few initiatives, each with a lead and a target date, with the dates that really matter marked as milestones. Risks, pending decisions and cross-team dependencies get their own labels and view, and a weekly update keeps everyone informed.

ux-design.name: UX design
ux-design.pitch: Take each design problem from research to a clean handoff, one clear phase at a time.
ux-design.description: A design workflow that follows each problem through research, definition, design, testing and handoff. Ready-made templates keep test rounds and handoffs quick, whiteboards hold journey maps and sketches, and every handoff ends with a walkthrough for engineering.
